subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Ventral wall defects and umbilical hernia
vignette: A newborn boy is delivered at term. There is a paraumbilical defect in the abdominal wall with loops of intestine protruding, and no covering membrane is visible. The defect lies to the right of the umbilicus and the infant is otherwise well.
question: Which ventral wall defect is characterized by abdominal contents protruding through an uncovered paraumbilical wall defect?
explanation_correct: Gastroschisis is a paraumbilical, usually right-sided full-thickness abdominal wall defect through which bowel herniates; the contents are not covered by peritoneum or amnion. It results from failure of lateral fold closure and is not commonly associated with chromosomal abnormalities, so prognosis is good. This contrasts with omphalocele, which is midline and covered by a shiny peritoneal/amniotic sac. The exposed bowel requires prompt surgical coverage.

explanation_incorrect.A: Omphalocele is a midline herniation through the umbilical ring covered by peritoneum and amnion (a shiny sac), unlike this uncovered paraumbilical defect.
explanation_incorrect.B: A congenital umbilical hernia is covered by skin, is usually reducible, and protrudes with crying; it is not an uncovered wall defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bladder exstrophy results from failed caudal fold closure and exposes the bladder rather than paraumbilical bowel.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ectopia cordis is a sternal defect from failed rostral fold closure in which the heart lies outside the chest.

educationalObjective: Gastroschisis is an uncovered, right-sided paraumbilical defect with a good prognosis and no strong chromosomal association.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Ventral wall defects and umbilical hernia
vignette: A fetus is found on prenatal ultrasound to have a midline abdominal wall defect with a membrane-covered sac containing liver and bowel. Postnatal examination shows a light gray, shiny sac. Genetic testing reveals trisomy 18.
question: Which ventral wall defect is midline, covered by peritoneum and amnion, and associated with trisomies 13 and 18?
explanation_correct: Omphalocele is herniation of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring, covered by peritoneum and amnion, producing a light gray shiny sac in the midline. It results from failed lateral fold closure and is associated with congenital anomalies including trisomies 13 and 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and cardiac, GU, and neural tube defects. The covering membrane plus a chromosomal anomaly points to omphalocele rather than gastroschisis. Associated anomalies strongly influence prognosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gastroschisis is paraumbilical and not covered by peritoneum or amnion, and it lacks the chromosomal associations described here.
explanation_incorrect.B: A congenital umbilical hernia is covered by skin rather than a shiny peritoneal/amniotic sac and is associated with Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bladder exstrophy is a caudal fold defect exposing the bladder, not a membrane-covered midline abdominal mass.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ectopia cordis is a rostral fold sternal defect with the heart exposed, not a midline umbilical sac.

educationalObjective: Omphalocele is a midline, membrane-covered defect associated with trisomies 13/18, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and other structural anomalies.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Ventral wall defects and umbilical hernia
vignette: A newborn is delivered with a sternal defect through which the heart protrudes outside the thoracic cavity. There is no associated abdominal wall herniation.
question: Failure of closure of which embryonic fold most directly causes ectopia cordis?
explanation_correct: Ventral wall defects arise from failure of specific body folds to close. Failure of rostral fold closure produces sternal defects such as ectopia cordis, in which the heart lies outside the thorax. Failure of lateral fold closure produces omphalocele and gastroschisis, while failure of caudal fold closure produces bladder exstrophy. Because the defect here is sternal with an exposed heart and no abdominal wall hernia, rostral fold closure failure is the answer. A defective pleuroperitoneal membrane instead causes congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

explanation_incorrect.B: Lateral fold closure failure causes omphalocele or gastroschisis, which are abdominal wall defects rather than a sternal heart defect.
explanation_incorrect.C: Caudal fold closure failure causes bladder exstrophy, not ectopia cordis.
explanation_incorrect.D: A defective pleuroperitoneal membrane causes congenital diaphragmatic hernia with abdominal contents in the chest, not an exposed heart.
explanation_incorrect.E: A patent umbilical ring underlies omphalocele and congenital umbilical hernia, not a sternal defect.

educationalObjective: Failed rostral fold closure causes ectopia cordis; lateral fold failure causes omphalocele/gastroschisis; caudal fold failure causes bladder exstrophy.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Ventral wall defects and umbilical hernia
vignette: A 2-year-old has a soft, skin-covered bulge at the umbilicus that appears when he cries and can be gently reduced into the abdomen. The mass was first noted after the physiologic midgut herniation resolved. He has Down syndrome.
question: Which defect results from delayed closure of the umbilical ring after physiologic herniation of the midgut?
explanation_correct: A congenital umbilical hernia is due to delayed closure of the umbilical ring after the physiologic herniation of the midgut, leaving a patent umbilical orifice. It is covered by skin, is often reducible, and protrudes with increased intra-abdominal pressure such as crying. It may be associated with Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism, and small defects usually close spontaneously. The skin covering and reducibility distinguish it from omphalocele and gastroschisis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Omphalocele is covered by peritoneum and amnion rather than skin, is present at birth as a shiny sac, and is associated with trisomies 13 and 18.
explanation_incorrect.C: Gastroschisis is an uncovered paraumbilical defect, not a skin-covered reducible umbilical bulge.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ectopia cordis is a rostral fold sternal defect with the heart exposed and is unrelated to the umbilical ring.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bladder exstrophy is a caudal fold defect exposing the bladder, not an umbilical hernia.

educationalObjective: Congenital umbilical hernia is a skin-covered, reducible bulge from delayed umbilical ring closure, linked to Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism.
